summary: Yogendra Miraje (Yogi), an AI Engineer at FactSet, presents lessons from building real-world plan-and-execute agents. He frames the challenge: AI applications feel like driving a monster truck through a crowded mall with a tiny joystick because agents lack the right context, especially enterprise-specific workflows. He defines an augmented LLM as an LLM combined with tools and memory; a workflow as an augmented LLM on a static predefined path; and an agent as an augmented LLM with high autonomy and feedback loops. He makes a critical distinction: a workflow agent is a predefined workflow run by an agent (workflow is in control, static), while an agentic workflow is a workflow planned and run by an agent (agent is in control, dynamic). On Andrew Ng's agentic spectrum, agentic workflows have more agenticness than workflow agents. For enterprises, agentic workflows enable automation at scale and leverage existing microservices investments. The key design pattern is planning by sub-goal division (task decomposition). FactSet adapted the LLM compiler architecture with components: blueprint generator (high-level natural-language plan), planner (low-level tasks), executor, and joiner (combines outputs, handles replanning with recursion limits). These run as nodes on LangGraph. The blueprint is a key architectural innovation—a series of natural-language steps fed to the planner—reducing cognitive overload, limiting in-context tools, aiding agentic behavior interpretation, and easing non-technical collaboration. Tool design around microservices requires thinking from the agent's perspective, providing tool purpose, description, and input/output contracts, plus validation checks as brakes. MCP is recommended for building standardized tool servers. Evals are essential: component and end-to-end evals using code-based checks, LLM-as-judge, and human-in-the-loop, with aspect-based evaluation for specific concerns like blueprint quality or tool selection. Agentic workflows should be avoided for fixed/repetitive tasks (use ETL), uncapturable workflows, deterministic-compliance needs, and low-latency/cost-sensitive environments. The talk closes with Q&A where Yogi notes that framework choice depends on the use case—multiple tools may be useful and the optimal framework varies by problem. He references LangChain for research paper code and suggests MCP for cross-organization standardization with LangGraph for orchestration.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Key Definitions
sections.summary: Yogi introduces himself as an AI Engineer at FactSet. He defines augmented LLM (LLM + tools + memory), workflow (augmented LLM on static path), and agent (augmented LLM with high autonomy and feedback loop). Workflows are controllable and reliable; agents are flexible and autonomous. The goal is getting the best of both worlds with agentic workflows.

sections.title: Workflow Agent vs Agentic Workflow Distinction
sections.summary: He makes a critical distinction: a workflow agent is a predefined workflow run by an agent (workflow in control, static), while an agentic workflow is a workflow planned and run by an agent (agent in control, dynamic). Referenced Andrew Ng's agentic spectrum. Enterprise value includes automation at scale and leveraging existing microservices.

sections.title: Building Agentic Workflows and Architecture
sections.summary: Advocates moving from react-based to proactive agents. Key design pattern: planning by sub-goal division (task decomposition). References specific research papers and LangChain blog with code. Describes FactSet's adapted LLM compiler architecture: blueprint generator, planner, executor, joiner as LangGraph nodes, with replanning logic and recursion limits.

sections.title: Tools and Microservices Design
sections.summary: Tool-microservice relationship is not one-to-one or many-to-one—it's up to the designer. Must think from the agent's perspective. Recommend MCP for standard tool servers. Provide tool purpose (what to select), description (when to invoke), input/output contracts (how to use), and validation checks as brakes.

sections.title: Blueprint Deep Dive
sections.summary: Blueprint is a natural-language series of steps fed to the planner. It reduces planner cognitive overload, limits in-context tools (avoiding context window issues), achieves final control over task planning, aids interpreting agentic behavior, and eases non-technical collaboration.

sections.title: Concrete Example and Evals
sections.summary: NVIDIA earnings call prep example: blueprint with tools and tasks (summarize, retrieve, reason, report). Before agentic workflow, responses are vanilla; after, they are structured. Evals are essential: component and end-to-end, using code-based (tool selection), LLM-as-judge (blueprint/plan alignment), human-in-the-loop (report formatting), and aspect-based evaluation.

sections.title: When Not to Use Agentic Workflows and Key Takeaways
sections.summary: Avoid agentic workflows for fixed/repetitive tasks (use ETL), uncapturable workflows, deterministic-compliance needs, and low-latency/cost environments. Key takeaways: agentic workflows are agent-planned, bring reliability at scale, use sub-goal division, plan-and-execute architecture, tools complement microservices, leverage research papers, and treat evals as first-class citizens.

sections.title: Q&A Closing
sections.summary: Final Q&A exchange on framework selection: Yogi notes multiple frameworks may be useful and the optimal choice depends on the use case. LangChain recommended for research paper code, MCP for cross-organization standardization, and LangGraph for orchestration. Talk concludes with thanks from the audience.

demonstrations: Financial research example: preparing for NVIDIA earnings call with blueprint steps (summarize previous earnings call, retrieve financial data, suggest questions, generate comprehensive report) and corresponding function calls

limitations: Not suitable for fixed and repetitive tasks—use ETL pipelines instead
Not appropriate when workflow cannot be captured in workflows

Avoid in low-latency and cost-sensitive environments
